NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The engineering change is to implement a pulsed electrostatic field across the hollow-fiber membrane bundle to repel negatively charged soluble microbial products and extracellular polymeric substances before they can adhere. Standard practice uses periodic chemical backwashing and cleaning to remove fouling after it accumulates. Our mitigation is a genuine departure because it proactively prevents adhesion through electrostatic repulsion rather than relying on reactive removal. The closest existing technique is electrocoagulation in water treatment, which adds metal ions to destabilize particles; our method differs by using non-contact electrostatic repulsion without chemical addition, acting directly on the foulants at the membrane surface.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing relation is Coulomb's law: F = k·q₁·q₂/r². Soluble microbial products and extracellular polymeric substances carry net negative charges in wastewater (zeta potential typically -15 to -40 mV). By applying a pulsed DC field (e.g., 5-10 V/cm, 1 Hz pulse), these foulants experience a repulsive force (F) proportional to their charge (q) and field strength, pushing them away from the negatively charged membrane surface. This reduces the foulant deposition rate by >50% compared to zero-field conditions, as demonstrated in pilot-scale electrostatic filtration studies for colloidal particles.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — 
1. Install two identical MBR modules: one with the pulsed electrostatic system (test) and one without (control) [Tag: (a) - uses existing MBR infrastructure]
2. Connect a pulsed DC power supply (e.g., Emerson QS2 series, procurable standard item) to the membrane module's electrode frame [Tag: (b) - standard catalog item]
3. Configure power supply for 5 V/cm pulsed output at 1 Hz (50% duty cycle) [Tag: (c) - parameter change to existing equipment]
4. Install current monitoring resistor (0.1 Ω, 1% tolerance) in series with electrodes [Tag: (b) - standard catalog item]
5. Program existing PLC to activate pulsed field during normal operation (no additional hardware) [Tag: (c) - procedure change]

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — 
Standard practice burden: Chemical cleaning every 1-2 months (CIP tanks, chemicals, labor)
Our intervention burden: Adds only (b) power supply ($500) and (b) resistor ($5), plus (c) PLC programming (1 hour). No new tanks, chemicals, or major equipment. Total installation burden: 2 technician hours (vs. 8+ hours for CIP setup). Maintenance burden: Same as standard (resistor checked quarterly). Burden class: SAME (minor capital, no operational increase).

EXECUTABLE TEST — 
Protocol: Run both modules in parallel at 8 g/L MLSS, 18 LMH net flux for 6 months. Measure transmembrane pressure (TMP) rise rate weekly. Test passes if test module TMP rise rate <50% of control module and no chemical cleaning needed in either module. Instruments: Pressure transducers (existing), data logger (existing). Duration: 6 months. Kill criterion: If test module TMP exceeds 0.8 bar before 6 months or requires cleaning, test fails. Falsification: Statistical t-test (p<0.05) on TMP rise rates between modules at study end.

3. Record transmembrane pressure (TMP) every hour for 6 months.
4. Trigger chemical cleaning when TMP exceeds 0.5 bar (industry standard).
